data.name: Mister Mart
data.detailed_description:
Check out our latest VR game!


Acerca do jogo

Enter the world of Mister Mart!
YOU are a customer service agent at a terrible grocery store. Because it's such a godawful grocery store, all of the customers are returning everything they've ever bought! In VR, use your hands to place the unwanted merchandise carefully into the return bin, but watch out! The customers loiter at your desk and will stress you out if you let them stay for too long! Use your Customer Service Fists (TM) to help them find the exit!

This game involves:
  • Customers!
  • Slapping Customers!
  • Raw Fish!
  • Hot Dogs!
  • Ragdoll Physics!

Mister Mart is played with the Oculus Rift CV1 and the Oculus Touch Controllers, with support for more VR systems and controllers on the way.

reviews.review:
Mister Mart takes one of the most ordinary settings imaginable, a grocery store customer service counter, and turns it into a deliberately ridiculous virtual reality playground. Developed and published by Studio217, LLC, it is less concerned with accurately simulating retail work than with transforming the frustrations of dealing with customers into physical comedy. Its straightforward concept makes it easy to understand almost immediately, while the VR interaction system supplies most of the personality and entertainment.

The basic job involves standing behind the customer service counter and processing merchandise brought back by customers. Returned products need to be grabbed and placed into the appropriate bins, creating a simple sorting challenge that becomes more demanding as customers accumulate around the counter. What begins as routine retail work quickly turns chaotic because shoppers have an inconvenient habit of remaining in the area after their business is finished. The solution is intentionally absurd: the player can physically shove, slap, or punch them away using motion-controlled hands.

This exaggerated approach is where the game finds most of its humor. Ragdoll physics turn interactions with customers into slapstick encounters, while ordinary grocery products become amusing objects to handle and toss around. Items such as fish and hot dogs reinforce the deliberately silly atmosphere. Rather than presenting aggressive interactions seriously, everything is framed as cartoonish workplace frustration taken to an impossible extreme. The physical nature of VR makes these simple actions more entertaining than they would probably be with traditional controls.

There is an arcade-style structure underneath all of the silliness. Efficiently handling returns and customers contributes to scoring, and leaderboard support encourages players to improve their performance across repeated sessions. Steam achievements provide another layer of objectives for completion-minded players. These systems are important because the underlying concept is intentionally limited. Once the novelty of physically dealing with unruly shoppers becomes familiar, improving scores and collecting achievements become the main incentives for returning.

Visually, Mister Mart adopts a colorful and exaggerated presentation that fits its comedic intentions. It does not attempt to create a realistic supermarket environment, nor does it need to. The store functions primarily as an interactive stage where merchandise, customers, physics, and the player's hands can collide in entertaining ways. The stylization also prevents the physical treatment of customers from feeling overly harsh, keeping the overall experience closer to a cartoon than a serious retail simulation.

Players expecting deep supermarket management should be aware of its limited scope. There are no elaborate economic systems, store expansions, staff-management mechanics, or detailed inventory operations forming the heart of the experience. Instead, the gameplay concentrates heavily on handling returns, keeping the customer area under control, and pursuing better scores. This focused design makes it suitable for shorter VR sessions but also limits the amount of mechanical variety available over longer periods.

Virtual reality is central to the design rather than an optional feature. The experience was originally built around VR headsets and tracked motion controllers, with standing and room-scale interaction forming an important part of gameplay. Physically reaching for merchandise and using your hands to interact with customers gives the game its distinctive character. Without that physical component, much of the comedy would lose its impact.

Steam Deck compatibility is effectively unsupported for normal handheld play. Mister Mart is a VR-focused title that requires appropriate virtual reality equipment and tracked controllers, while the Steam Deck itself does not provide the required native VR setup. Even if technical experimentation were possible through external equipment, this should not be considered a practical Steam Deck game. Anyone specifically seeking something to play directly on the Deck's screen with its built-in controls should look elsewhere.

The game's greatest strength is its willingness to commit completely to a simple and absurd idea. Sorting returned groceries could have been painfully mundane, but adding troublesome customers, exaggerated physics, motion controls, and arcade scoring turns it into an unusual VR comedy. Its greatest weakness is that the same focused premise naturally restricts variety. Players who enjoy ragdoll physics and short score-driven VR experiences are likely to get considerably more entertainment from it than those searching for progression, narrative depth, or sophisticated simulation mechanics.

Mister Mart ultimately succeeds as a compact piece of VR slapstick built around the universal frustration of customer service. It does not try to become a sprawling supermarket simulator and instead concentrates on tactile interaction, chaotic customers, humorous physics, achievements, and score chasing. The experience may be modest in scale, but its unusual premise gives it a memorable identity. For VR players who appreciate deliberately silly physics games and do not mind repetitive mechanics, it can provide an amusing diversion that knows exactly what kind of experience it wants to deliver.

Rating: 6/10
